Quotation guidance:

"""
# Quoting speech

Read this before putting quotation marks around anything somebody said. It applies to interview transcripts, recorded remarks, meeting notes, and any other material where the words are a person's rather than a document's.

Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.

When translating permitted quotations, preserve meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice in idiomatic target-language speech, not source-language syntax. The restrictions below protect that substance; they do not require word-for-word translation. Make an implicit referent explicit only when the supplied context settles it. Where the meaning remains ambiguous, paraphrase what is established rather than inventing a fluent interpretation.

## What may be repaired

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

## What may not

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.

**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.

## When to paraphrase instead

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.

Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.

## What stays outside this

Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved.

5	## Brief
6	
7	Write a journalistic customer case for operations managers at small housing companies. The publisher is the supplier, Svale Systems. The customer, Elm Quay Housing, should remain the acting party. Approximately 400 words, as material allows. Markdown. No author name supplied. The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read, not a consultation booking or a product trial.

9	## Material
10	
11	Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats. In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings. Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately. The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information. It chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available.
12	
13	The maintenance team designed its categories and kept telephone reporting open for residents. Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions. The trial lasted eight weeks. Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial. Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period. The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software. There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements.
14

16	
17	- “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.”
18	- “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”
19	- “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”
20

All interviews occurred by email, and no physical scene, emotion or remembered dialogue is provided. Translation of the quotations is permitted, preserving stance and qualification.
22

## A. Claim-by-claim accounting

Each item gives the draft passage (D), the source passage (S) and the comparison.

**A1. Title.** D: "Elm Quay's repair trial gives shifts one view".
S: "The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information." and Lind: "We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done." and "Having one view of the reports helps us".
Difference: the source gives shifts sharing information only as the team's aim. It shows that one view exists only through Lind's "one view of the reports helps us", where "us" means the team, not the shifts. The title turns the aim into an achieved result for the shifts. See **F1**.

**A2. Dek, sentence 1.** D: "Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 apartments, tested a shared repair log from Svale Systems in two of its buildings."
S: "Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats. In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings." and "It chose Svale Systems".
Difference: "flats" and "apartments" name the same thing in en_US. "Its buildings" means buildings that Elm Quay manages. Nothing in this context separates managing from owning in a way that changes the claim. Supported.

**A3. Dek, sentence 2, first part.** D: "Its maintenance supervisor would run the trial again, with an extra week for preparation".
S: "I would choose to do the trial again. … but I would leave an extra week for preparation." and "Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind".
Difference: none of substance. The conditional "would" is kept, and the extra week is stated. Supported.

**A4. Dek, sentence 2, second part.** D: "—a lesson for any operations manager planning something similar."
S: no source passage. The draft generalises Lind's own intention ("I would leave an extra week").
Assessment: this is the author's framing, resting on a supported quotation. It concerns preparation time, not a recommendation of Svale, so it does not contradict "Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company." It is not a defect. It is an **editorial question (E1)**: "any" presents Lind's personal plan as general advice, which the material does not give as anybody's position.

**A5. Paragraph 1, sentence 1.** D: "Repair reports at Elm Quay Housing used to arrive by telephone and by email, and the two were stored separately."
S: "Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately." and "kept telephone reporting open for residents."
Difference: in the source, "previously" applies only to the separate storage. In the draft, "used to" also governs the arrival channels, which implies that reports no longer arrive by telephone. The source says telephone reporting stayed open. See **F2**.

**A6. Paragraph 1, sentence 2.** D: "In September 2025 the company's own maintenance team decided to test a shared log in two buildings so that staff on different shifts could see the same information."
S: "In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings. … The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information." Also Lind: "We wanted the evening shift to see…".
Difference: the draft turns "wanted" into a purpose clause ("so that"). The team's stated want and Lind's "We wanted" support it as the motive. The date, the team and the scope match. Supported.

**A7. Paragraph 1, sentence 3.** D: "After the eight-week trial, the team had a figure its own trial note does not credit to the software and a verdict from its supervisor that comes with a condition."
S: "The trial lasted eight weeks. Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025 … the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software." and "Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment."
Differences:
- (a) The pronoun "its" is third-person singular and non-personal, referring to "the team". "Its own trial note" therefore makes the maintenance team the owner or author of the note. The source says only "Elm Quay's internal trial note". See **F3**.
- (b) "Comes with a condition": the source calls the assessment "qualified", and Lind's wording is "but I would leave an extra week". The draft upgrades her reservation to a condition. See **F4**.
- (c) "After the eight-week trial": the note compares "during the trial" with "the preceding eight-week period", which fits a note written after the trial. This is not a finding.
- (d) "Its supervisor": the pronoun refers to the team, and Lind is the maintenance supervisor. Supported.

**A8. Heading.** D: "Elm Quay tested repair tracking before picking Svale".
S: "It chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair."
Difference: "repair tracking" is a fair short form of whether the log could show "the status of each repair". The order (test first, then choice) matches the source. Supported.

**A9. Quotation and frame.** D: "In an email interview, maintenance supervisor Maya Lind puts the aim concretely: 'We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done.'"
S: "All interviews occurred by email" and quotation 1, first sentence (verbatim).
Difference: none. The draft splits quotation 1 into two separate quotations, each verbatim, and does not weld any remarks together. "Puts the aim concretely" is an accurate characterisation of the sentence. Supported.

**A10. Choice of supplier.** D: "The team chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available."
S: the same words. Supported.

**A11. Heading.** D: "Elm Quay designed the categories, and Svale set up the system".
S: "The maintenance team designed its categories … Svale configured the log".
Difference: "set up the system" and "configured the log" name the same act in this context. "Elm Quay" stands for its own maintenance team. Supported.

**A12. Telephone route.** D: "Residents kept the option of reporting repairs by telephone; the team left that route open."
S: "kept telephone reporting open for residents." Supported.

**A13. Configuration, training and quotation.** D: "Svale Systems configured the log and trained six staff members in two sessions, and Lind is precise about the division of work: 'The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.'"
S: "Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions." and quotation 1, second sentence (verbatim).
Difference: none. "Precise" is the author's reading of a quotation that visibly divides the work. Supported.

**A14. Categories quotation.** D: "Lind draws a practical lesson from the work: 'We spent more time … before the next building starts.'"
S: quotation 2, verbatim. Supported.

**A15. Heading.** D: "Trial note records faster assignment but claims no cause".
S: "Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period." "It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial." "The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
Differences:
- (a) "Faster assignment" drops "median" and the exclusions. See **F5**.
- (b) "Claims no cause" is broader than "does not attribute the difference to the software". See **F6**.

**A16. Trial note.** D: "Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial."
S: the same content. The date is only reformatted for en_US. The pronoun "It" is third-person singular and refers to the note, as in the source. Supported.

**A17. Assignment times.** D: "Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial, against three in the preceding eight-week period. The two periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
S: the same content. Supported.

**A18. Completion and other measures.** D: "Nor is assignment the same as completion. There are no measurements of completion time, cost, or resident satisfaction."
S: "There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements." and the brief: "Do not turn assignment time into completion time."
Difference: none. The first sentence is the author's clarification and makes no factual claim. Supported.

**A19. Heading.** D: "The supervisor would repeat the trial with more preparation".
S: "I would choose to do the trial again. … I would leave an extra week for preparation."
Difference: "More preparation" corresponds to the extra week, and "would" keeps the conditional. It describes what she would do and does not make preparation a precondition. Supported.

**A20. Final assessment.** D: "Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company. The assessment Lind does give is a qualified one, and it is not drawn from the figures: 'I would choose to do the trial again. …'"
S: "Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company. Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment. It is not an inference from the figures." and quotation 3, verbatim.
Difference: none. The customer's reservation is kept. Supported.

**A21. Heading.** D: "Expansion waits on a check of larger repairs".
S: "The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs."
Difference: the object of the check has changed, and the heading presupposes expansion where the source has only a pending decision. See **F7**.

**A22. Expansion decision.** D: "The trial has not yet expanded. The team will decide after checking how its categories work for larger repairs."
S: the same content. "Its" refers to the team. The source says "the categories", and elsewhere "The maintenance team designed its categories". Supported.

**A23. Summary sentence.** D: "That leaves Elm Quay with a shared view its supervisor says helps, a figure its note does not credit to the software, and a decision still ahead."
S: "Having one view of the reports helps us" and "Elm Quay's internal trial note … does not attribute the difference to the software." and "the team will decide".
Difference: "its" refers to Elm Quay here, which matches "Elm Quay's internal trial note". Supported.

**A24. Link.** D: "For operations managers weighing a similar trial, [read the implementation checklist](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist)."
S: "The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read".
Difference: none. The link text accurately describes its destination. Supported.

### Pronouns: person, number and natural gender

- **Narrative pronouns.** The draft uses only third-person singular non-personal "its" and "it", for Elm Quay, the team and the note. It uses no gendered pronoun for Lind anywhere. The source's "Her" (natural gender, female) is not carried over, and no gender is asserted, so nothing conflicts.
- **"Its own trial note" (A7a).** This assigns possession to the team rather than to Elm Quay. That is a question of referent and whose document it is, handled in F3.
- **Pronouns inside quotations.** "We", "ours", "us" and "I" are first person, singular and plural as in the source. The quotations are reproduced verbatim, so person and number are unchanged.
- **Grammatical gender.** Not applicable: the draft is in English.

## B. Findings (source support)

**F1. The title turns the aim into an achieved result.**
- Draft: "Elm Quay's repair trial gives shifts one view".
- Support: the source gives shift-sharing only as a wish ("The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information"). Lind attests only that "Having one view of the reports helps us".
- Case: the log gives the team a single view of reports, but the evening shift in practice does not see the morning shift's work. Nothing in the material says the shifts actually saw the same information, and no supplied statement excludes this case.
- Repair: "Elm Quay's repair trial sought to give shifts one view". Alternatively, "Elm Quay's repair trial gives its team one view of reports", which rests on Lind's quotation.

**F2. "Used to" implies that telephone reporting stopped.**
- Draft: "Repair reports at Elm Quay Housing used to arrive by telephone and by email, and the two were stored separately."
- Support: the source puts only the storage in the past ("Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately"). It also says the team "kept telephone reporting open for residents".
- Case: residents still phone in repair reports during and after the trial. The source's "kept telephone reporting open" leaves this compatible, and the draft's "used to arrive" makes it false.
- Repair: "Before the trial, repair reports that reached Elm Quay Housing by telephone and by email were stored separately."

**F3. The trial note is attributed to the team.**
- Draft: "the team had a figure its own trial note does not credit to the software".
- Support: "Elm Quay's internal trial note". The source does not say the maintenance team wrote or owns it.
- Case: the note was written by Elm Quay management outside the maintenance team. This is compatible with the source, which the draft's "its own" then misstates.
- Repair: "the team had a figure that Elm Quay's own trial note does not credit to the software". Alternatively, "…a figure the company's trial note does not credit to the software".

**F4. The qualification becomes a condition.**
- Draft: "a verdict from its supervisor that comes with a condition".
- Support: "Her final quotation is her actual, qualified assessment", and her wording is "I would choose to do the trial again. … but I would leave an extra week for preparation."
- Case: Lind would repeat the trial even if the extra week were not available, and simply plans to add it. Her words are compatible with this, and "condition" then fails.
- Repair: "a verdict from its supervisor that comes with a qualification", or "…with a reservation".

**F5. The heading drops "median" and the exclusions.**
- Draft: "Trial note records faster assignment…".
- Support: "Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period." and "It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial."
- Case: emergency repairs, which the note excludes, were assigned more slowly during the trial, while the median for the 31 recorded reports fell. "Faster assignment" as a general claim then fails, and nothing in the material excludes this case.
- Repair: "Trial note records a shorter median assignment time…".

**F6. "Claims no cause" is broader than the note's stated position.**
- Draft: "…but claims no cause".
- Support: "the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software." The material does not say that the note attributes the difference to nothing at all.
- Case: the note attributes the difference to the lighter workload of the trial period. This is compatible with "The periods had different workloads", and the draft's "claims no cause" then fails.
- Repair: "…but does not credit the software".

**F7. The heading presupposes expansion and changes what is checked.**
- Draft: "Expansion waits on a check of larger repairs".
- Support: "The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs."
- Case 1: after the check, the team decides not to expand. This is compatible with "will decide", yet the heading implies expansion is only waiting.
- Case 2: the larger repairs themselves are fine, but the categories do not fit them. The draft's "check of larger repairs" names the repairs as the thing checked, whereas the source's check is of the categories.
- Repair: "Expansion decision waits on how the categories handle larger repairs".

## C. Editorial question (not a defect)

**E1.** Dek: "—a lesson for any operations manager planning something similar." This is the author's generalisation of Lind's personal plan ("I would leave an extra week for preparation"). The brief does not give it as the commissioning party's position, and the material does not generalise it. It is defensible as the author's reflection, because it concerns preparation, not a recommendation of Svale. The editor may prefer "a lesson Lind draws for the next building".

## D. Translation findings

None. The draft is in the source language, and all four quotations are verbatim. Quotation 1 is split into two verbatim parts, with no welding and no change of meaning.

## Completion status

Complete. All claims in the title, dek, body, headings and link are accounted for. There are seven unresolved source-support findings, F1 to F7. F2, F5, F6 and F7 are the most consequential, because each changes scope, cause or outcome; F1, F3 and F4 are minor. There is one editorial question (E1) and no translation findings.
